Ethiopian catchment studies cited in a review report physical soil and water conservation decreasing runoff by up to 88% (Taye et al., 2015; Haregeweyn et al., 2015), and integrated catchment management at May Zeg Zeg cutting surface runoff volume by 81% (Nyssen et al., 2010) [ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_7, ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_8].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Nearly all units are programme or lender reports from Ethiopia, India and China, often perception surveys or before/after comparisons; an Uttarakhand water budget showed surface runoff slightly increasing, the Karnataka runoff comparison is against another SWC programme, and IEG doubts the India runoff measurements. Effects mixing runoff and soil-loss metrics are only components of erosion risk. A catchment-restoration meta-analysis in Ethiopia finds minimal effect of catchment treatment on runoff in drought-prone areas with annual rainfall below 500 mm [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_3]. The Ethiopian catchment results combine structures with grazing control and vegetation regeneration and are cited in a review, so the share due to the works is not isolated [ev_erosion_hazard_meko14_1]. The 88% and 81% runoff figures are cited second-hand: the first is an upper bound, and the second is a before-and-after result for a catchment-management package rather than the structures alone [ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_7, ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_8].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Sediment-control dams, terraces and vegetation in a Loess Plateau watershed programme capture sediment each year, reducing the load reaching downstream rivers.
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Single modelled programme-level estimate from a lender review in China, using sediment retention as a proxy for water quality.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Watershed treatment reduces reliance on outside supply: participating villages in India saw reduced water transportation by tanker compared with nonparticipating villages [ev_water_access_deficit_verm19_1], and an agency review credits consumption and production cisterns in semi-arid Brazil with a significant contribution to wider access to water [ev_water_access_deficit_castro22_1]. In India, discharge of springs and streams rose in treated watersheds: a sample study in Himachal Pradesh reports a 40 percent increase in water discharge in spring and stream sources [ev_water_regulation_hp17_1], and the Uttarakhand project achieved an average 21 percent increase in water discharge from perennial water sources in sampled micro-watersheds, against a target of 25 percent [ev_water_regulation_utk22_6]. Measured soil moisture adds a field route: a meta-analysis of in-situ practices finds they improve soil moisture retention by 59%, with soil/stone bunds at an SMD of 76.4% [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_1, ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_3]; in Burkina Faso zaï of 30–40 cm diameter and 1-m half-moons retained moisture for 2-3 weeks through dry spells [ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7]; and Indian project watersheds showed an increase in soil moisture content by 30.5 percent compared to the IWMP sites [ev_soil_water_retention_kar20_2]. Water productivity, the grain produced per unit of rain, is a route by which capture eases water stress. The water-productivity evidence points the same way: FAO compilers list improved water use efficiency among the main benefits of rainwater harvesting, the WOCAT guideline authors find that all water harvesting groups indicate improved water use efficiency, mostly high to medium, through reduced evaporation loss and better soil water availability, and a review sentence, citing earlier work, says capture approaches often lead also to higher water productivity because denser canopies shade the soil [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The tanker reduction is a reported programme assessment [ev_water_access_deficit_verm19_1], and the Brazilian unit is an agency inference from census figures in an upper-middle-income context [ev_water_access_deficit_castro22_1]. The Indian spring and stream discharge figures come from World Bank completion reports, the lender's own evaluation, measured before and after without untreated comparison sites, for catchment treatment that bundles plantations, trenches, ponds and check dams with water-harvesting structures, so the gain cannot be credited to water harvesting alone [ev_water_regulation_hp17_1, ev_water_regulation_utk22_6]. Groundwater-recharge evidence, with its limits, now sits in the catchment water yield rows, which also answer what upstream capture does to water downstream. The pooled 59% covers mixed in-situ practices, and the zaï and half-moon result comes with compost in the pits, so neither credits a single structure [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_1, ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7]. The Indian soil-moisture comparison is a project-commissioned study of a package of soil and water conservation structures [ev_soil_water_retention_kar20_2]. These are compiler and author judgements across groups, direction only, and the review sentence is second-hand; the WOCAT authors also note that some case studies indicate little to no improvement in water use efficiency [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers for zaï or tassa planting pits and contour bunds in Niger, planting pits in Uganda and conservation tillage with the Magoye ripper in Zambia judge the technologies to cope well with drought [ev_asset_drought_wocat_1219_2014_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1652_2014_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1587_2013_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1139_2013_drought].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: All units are practitioner judgements from documented technology sheets, not measurements, with no observed damage or failure data behind them. These are field-level practices, so the ratings describe how the treated fields fare under drought rather than damage to a built structure.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Heavy rain overtops or knocks down small field structures: tied ridges in a Kenyan trial collapsed during heavy rainfall events and had to be rebuilt within the season, staggered earth bunds (tabia) in Morocco store the runoff of rains below 50 mm, but in the biggest storms the excess overtops the bunds and gullies the slope [ev_climate_shock_roos10_1_av], and WOCAT compilers rate zaï or tassa pits and contour bunds in Niger as not coping well with local rainstorms [ev_climate_shock_ndun23_1_av, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1219_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1652_2014_local_rainstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The Ugandan planting-pit compiler rates coping as good [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1587_2013_local_rainstorm]. The Kenyan observation comes from a single-site trial and records rebuilding rather than a loss figure, the Moroccan statement is from a technique manual, and the remaining units are practitioner ratings without damage records [ev_climate_shock_ndun23_1_av, ev_climate_shock_roos10_1_av].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers judge zaï or tassa planting pits and contour bunds in Niger not to cope well with general river floods [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1219_2014_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1652_2014_general_river_flood].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are practitioner judgements from documented technology sheets, all from Niger, with no observed loss or failure data [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1219_2014_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1652_2014_general_river_flood]. Pits and bunds are field-level practices, so a not-well rating describes exposure of the treated fields to floodwater rather than damage to a built structure.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers judge zaï or tassa planting pits and contour bunds in Niger and planting pits in Uganda to cope well with local windstorms; no unit describes how wind would damage them [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1219_2014_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1652_2014_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1587_2013_local_windstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are three practitioner judgements from documented technology sheets with no observed damage data. Pits and bunds are field-level practices, so the ratings describe exposure of the treated fields rather than damage to a built structure.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The proximity of zai pits on crusted, degraded soil raises the chances of seed germination and dispersal, so herbaceous and woody species recolonise formerly bare land in Burkina Faso [ev_biodiversity_outcome_roose93_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_zoug14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_kabo04_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The Burkina Faso evidence is descriptive, without an untreated comparison, and partly the same observation cited more than once. None of the units gives a size for the gain in species, so the strength is not quantified, and the evidence covers zai on degraded land in a single semi-arid country [ev_biodiversity_outcome_roose93_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_zoug14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_kabo04_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field practices store carbon in the soil as organic matter builds up where water and organic inputs are held: zai fields in Burkina Faso treated for several years had higher organic matter and trenches combined with vegetation raised soil organic carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kabo04_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese soil and water conservation measures, available as a preprint, finds soil organic carbon 10.74% to 22.63% above the initial level after straw mulching across regions, and 3.36% and 75.77% higher after contour tillage in two regions within 5 to 10 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_4].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The evidence is mixed: trenches in Mexico reduced soil nitrogen and carbon, and a zai trial in Burkina Faso detected no significant change in organic matter even though biomass production rose [ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_roose93_1]. The size of the gain rests on the Chinese figures, which come from a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, in an upper-middle-income country, and cover straw mulching and contour tillage rather than pits or trenches; the contour-tillage values are for the 5-to-10-year window with the greatest increase, not a pooled estimate [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_4]. Paired soil samples from Zambian fields under planting basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with crop residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in organic carbon from conventional fields [ev_soil_organic_carbon_umar11_4].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In the Maghreb, mechanised bund systems, built with large machines that scrape a 4 to 10 m strip to raise bunds 1.5 to 2 m high every 30 to 50 m, considerably reduce the water collected in downstream hill reservoirs and cost 10 to 25% of the cultivable area [ev_water_yield_roos10_1]. On the other side, earth and stone bunds in Mauritania were built to facilitate water infiltration and replenish groundwater tables, and surveyed communities expressed satisfaction with the rising levels of water in their wells [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mrt14_1]; in the Peruvian Andes a few studies have observed catchment-level changes such as increased aquifer recharge, which the source calls plausible but not generalisable [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_locat20_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks what capturing water upstream does to the water that reaches streams and reservoirs below, not whether the farm that captures it has more. The sides are measured in different places: the gains are well levels and recharge around the treated land, the loss is water reaching downstream hill reservoirs below mechanised bunds, and a downstream loss can coexist with the local gain. The source ties the loss to mechanised construction and cites it from earlier work in an expert manual; the Mauritanian gain is a lender-reported community perception for works that also included fencing [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mrt14_1]; and in the Peruvian Andes trenches had little effect on increasing baseflow, with hydrogeological characteristics key to explaining their impact [ev_water_regulation_locat20_1]. No finding is quantified.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field practices that replace tillage can cut recurrent farm costs: in Mozambique labour costs were $153 per hectare for basins against $173 under conventional tillage, and mulching reduced weed density and labour costs for weeding in an Ethiopian trial [ev_project_cost_kida19_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The savings are in recurrent costs, not the cost of building anything. Where the practice adds earthworks the cost rises: switching from flat-land production to tied ridges, with or without grass strips, increased the cost of production in Ghana's Nandom area [ev_project_cost_dalt14_2]. The Mozambique basins also carry residue retention and herbicide weed control, and the Ethiopian and Ghana statements give no cost figure [ev_project_cost_kida19_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1, ev_project_cost_dalt14_2].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field pits raise infiltration and water retention so crops suffer less from dry spells: zaï gave 300–400 kg of sorghum per hectare in a low-rainfall year on degraded land where the without-zaï yield was 0, only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger, zaï trials let cereals be grown on degraded crusted soils with honourable yields in rainfall-deficit periods, and chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s, ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Studies cited in conservation agriculture meta-analyses report yields 10–100% higher than conventional tillage in relatively dry years [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks where soil water storage reaches 50 mm [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. Conservation agriculture pillars had no detectable effect on maize in a Kenyan season with a failed start, and a cited study reports conservation agriculture yields 5–20% lower in wet years [ev_crop_yield_boil19_3, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4]. The strongest results are practitioner-reported contrasts from a single Sahelian report, and the conservation agriculture dry-year findings are secondary citations inside meta-analyses rather than pooled estimates [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zaï and tassa pits increase infiltration and the water retention capacity of the soil, so crops suffer less from drought spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In rainfall-deficit periods zaï allowed cereals to be grown on degraded crusted soils in Burkina Faso, gave sorghum in a low-rainfall year where untreated land yielded nothing, and only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger [ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s]. In Malawi's El Niño drought season ground cover (a soil-cover mulch, modelled separately from the other practices) raised maize from 247 kg per hectare on control plots to 432 kg per hectare and raised the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1]. In Zimbabwe first-year planting-basin farmers obtained 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 368 kg on conventional plots in the 2006/07 season, which the source calls a drought year [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1]. In a Kenyan trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 2.53 against 1.82 t per hectare without inputs (not significant) and 4.10 against 3.15 t per hectare with manure and fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3]. Chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Against the fertilised conventional arm in the same Zimbabwe budget the contrast was 1520 against 400 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, the plots without mulch were the ones particularly affected by the dry spells of the season [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. In on-farm conservation-farming trials in Kenya, Tanzania and Ethiopia the largest yield difference over conventional ploughing came in rainy seasons with low rainfall, when the practice maximises rainfall infiltration so the crop can bridge short periods of dry spell [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season of very scattered rainfall, maize in hand-hoe conservation-farming basins yielded 3,054 kg per hectare against 1,339 kg under ploughing, which the authors say showcased the water-harvesting benefits of the basins [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1]. Farmers practising basins in Zambia, Zimbabwe and Limpopo reported maize and sorghum yields of >1 tonnes per hectare even in seasons with poor rainfall (<450 mm), against total crop failure under conventional ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields too [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. In semi-arid north-east Nigeria, tied ridging with a wood-shavings mulch raised sorghum grain yield by 67% over a flat bed in 1999, a season that ended in drought at grain filling [ev_crop_yield_chir06_6]. In southern Malawi's 2015/16 El Niño season, maize hybrids under conservation agriculture (planting in small holes with residue cover) yielded 700 kg per hectare more on average than under conventional ridge tillage [ev_crop_yield_seti18_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks, and only where soil water storage capacity is at least 50 mm [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In the Kenyan trial's short rains with meteorological droughts, tied ridging gave no advantage (0.52 against 0.53 t per hectare without inputs, 1.17 against 1.27 with manure and fertiliser) because there was little or no rainwater to hold in the basins [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_4, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_soil_water_retention_ndun23_1]. In Mozambique no cowpea yield was obtained on any treatment in a season heavily affected by drought [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_2]. The family rests partly on on-farm or trial measurements in Malawi, Kenya, Zimbabwe and Mozambique; the zaï and tassa contrasts are author estimates, the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the Kenyan tied-ridging result is a single-site trial [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1]. Not every in-field practice helped in that Malawi El Nino season: banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare and lowered the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054 [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5, ev_food_security_boil19_3]. The Ethiopian dry-spell finding is a field observation of which plots wilted, not a tested yield contrast [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. Water harvesting is not irrigation, and the new primaries mark the limit: at the more arid Kenyan sites of Laikipia and Machakos each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, with 0 kg per hectare of maize harvested at Machakos due to meteorological drought, and the conservation-farming treatments did not avert it [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. In the Zimbabwe panel conservation agriculture had no specific impact in mitigating rainfall-shortfall losses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. The East African low-rainfall gain is for the best system per site, ripping or pitting usually with fertiliser, so it is bundled with reduced tillage and fertiliser, and the authors read it as a trend from their own figure [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. The Zambia 2001/2 basin contrast is a raw comparison in a single season with no normal-year reference, and most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit, so part of the gap is the input package [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1]. The farmer-reported basin yields compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author warns makes those datasets too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The Zimbabwe panel's drought-season gains are interaction estimates for conservation agriculture as practised (planting basins bundled with residue mulch and rotation); its normal-season results are reported in the production row, not here [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zaï and tassa pits increase infiltration and the water retention capacity of the soil, so crops suffer less from drought spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In rainfall-deficit periods zaï allowed cereals to be grown on degraded crusted soils in Burkina Faso, gave sorghum in a low-rainfall year where untreated land yielded nothing, and only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger [ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s]. In Malawi's El Niño drought season ground cover (a soil-cover mulch, modelled separately from the other practices) raised maize from 247 kg per hectare on control plots to 432 kg per hectare and raised the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1]. Chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Farmers practising basins in Zambia, Zimbabwe and Limpopo reported maize and sorghum yields of >1 tonnes per hectare even in seasons with poor rainfall (<450 mm), against total crop failure under conventional ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields too [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. In Nigeria, tied ridging with wood-shavings mulch raised sorghum grain yield over the flat bed by 67% in 1999 [ev_crop_yield_chir06_6], and in Malawi maize under conservation agriculture produced 700 kg per hectare more grain than conventional practice in 2015/16 [ev_crop_yield_seti18_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks, and only where soil water storage capacity is at least 50 mm, so it does not address seasonal drought [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In Mozambique no cowpea yield was obtained on any treatment in a season heavily affected by drought [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_2]. The Malawi on-farm survey of ground cover gives measured support, while the zaï and tassa yield contrasts are author estimates [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s]. Not every in-field practice helped in that Malawi El Nino season: banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare and lowered the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054 [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5, ev_food_security_boil19_3]. In the Zimbabwe panel conservation agriculture had no specific impact in mitigating rainfall-shortfall losses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. The farmer-reported basin yields compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author warns makes those datasets too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The Zimbabwe panel's drought-season gains are interaction estimates for conservation agriculture as practised (planting basins bundled with residue mulch and rotation); its normal-season results are reported in the production row, not here [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. The Nigerian ridging gain bundles the tied ridges with mulch [ev_crop_yield_chir06_6].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zaï and tassa pits increase infiltration and the water retention capacity of the soil, so crops suffer less from drought spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In rainfall-deficit periods zaï allowed cereals to be grown on degraded crusted soils in Burkina Faso, gave sorghum in a low-rainfall year where untreated land yielded nothing, and only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger [ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s]. In Zimbabwe first-year planting-basin farmers obtained 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 368 kg on conventional plots in the 2006/07 season, which the source calls a drought year [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1]. In a Kenyan trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 2.53 against 1.82 t per hectare without inputs (not significant) and 4.10 against 3.15 t per hectare with manure and fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3]. Chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Against the fertilised conventional arm in the same Zimbabwe budget the contrast was 1520 against 400 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, the plots without mulch were the ones particularly affected by the dry spells of the season [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. In on-farm conservation-farming trials in Kenya, Tanzania and Ethiopia the largest yield difference over conventional ploughing came in rainy seasons with low rainfall, when the practice maximises rainfall infiltration so the crop can bridge short periods of dry spell [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season of very scattered rainfall, maize in hand-hoe conservation-farming basins yielded 3,054 kg per hectare against 1,339 kg under ploughing, which the authors say showcased the water-harvesting benefits of the basins [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks, and only where soil water storage capacity is at least 50 mm [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In the Kenyan trial's short rains with meteorological droughts, tied ridging gave no advantage (0.52 against 0.53 t per hectare without inputs, 1.17 against 1.27 with manure and fertiliser) because there was little or no rainwater to hold in the basins [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_4, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_soil_water_retention_ndun23_1]. The zaï and tassa contrasts are author estimates, the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the Kenyan tied-ridging result comes from a single-site trial [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1]. The Ethiopian dry-spell finding is a field observation of which plots wilted, not a tested yield contrast [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. Water harvesting is not irrigation, and the new primaries mark the limit: at the more arid Kenyan sites of Laikipia and Machakos each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, with 0 kg per hectare of maize harvested at Machakos due to meteorological drought, and the conservation-farming treatments did not avert it [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The East African low-rainfall gain is for the best system per site, ripping or pitting usually with fertiliser, so it is bundled with reduced tillage and fertiliser, and the authors read it as a trend from their own figure [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. The Zambia 2001/2 basin contrast is a raw comparison in a single season with no normal-year reference, and most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit, so part of the gap is the input package [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zai pits concentrate runoff into the root zone, so crops can ride out a dry spell of two to three weeks. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, the plots without mulch were the ones particularly affected by the dry spells of the season [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: An expert statement from Burkina Faso, explicitly conditional on the soil having sufficient water storage capacity [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1], and an Ethiopian field observation of which plots wilted in dry spells, not a tested contrast [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Infiltration trenches catch runoff on the slope: every reviewed study that measured plot runoff found less runoff with trenches, and on average trenches cut runoff by 46.4%, equal to 5.7% of rainfall, a result the review files under runoff and flood reduction [ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The row rests on a single review of plot-scale runoff from Andean mountain studies; it measures runoff, not flood peaks, flood damage or crop losses in floods, so the link to flood impact on livelihoods is a component proxy, and with one source there is nothing to test agreement against. No unit covers severe or extreme floods [ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers for planting pits and stone lines, zai/tassa pits and contour bunds in Niger and conservation tillage in Kenya and Zambia judge downstream flooding reduced; the sheets describe no mechanism, and the Zambia compiler adds that the effect holds only if the practice is applied on a large scale.
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: All units are practitioner judgements, not measurements, mostly rated slight; the conservation-tillage sheet from the Philippines rated flood impacts worse, and conservation-tillage sheets are a loose fit for an in-situ water-harvesting family.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Planting basins and ground cover hold rain where crops grow, raising staple harvests. Planting basins (zai pits) raised the odds of a Kenyan plot meeting the household maize requirement to 421.75 against 1.67 in the control, and ground cover raised those odds in Malawi's El Nino season [ev_food_security_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Practice choice and season matter. In the same Malawian El Nino season, banking lowered the odds of meeting the maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054, so a mis-matched in-field practice can deepen food shortfall [ev_food_security_boil19_3]. The large Kenyan odds come from an above-average rainfall season and do not show performance in drought [ev_food_security_boil19_2]. Every unit comes from the same study, a plot-level analysis of yield thresholds rather than a household food-security survey, which is why the strong class stands on a narrow base.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: A maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture performs better relative to conventional practice under drought and/or heat stress, the in-field mulch and reduced tillage carrying the effect [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single meta-analytic statement for maize that does not separate heat from drought and gives no magnitude in the quoted passage, so the heat-specific effect is not isolated [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: A maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture performs better relative to conventional practice under drought and/or heat stress, the in-field mulch and reduced tillage carrying the effect [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single meta-analytic statement for maize that does not separate heat from drought and gives no magnitude in the quoted passage, so the heat-specific effect is not isolated [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Planting pits (zai, tassa), tied ridges and furrows, mulch, basin tillage and infiltration trenches capture runoff near the plants; combined with manure they let cereals be grown on degraded crusted soils, and in the 1990 drought in Niger only tassa fields produced a harvest. Meta-analyses quantify the gain: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds yield increases of 142% for infiltration pits, 91% for mulching and 74% for tied ridging over controls [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_2, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_3, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_6]; and a synthesis of Ethiopian studies gives mean grain-yield differences of 554.3 kg per hectare for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4]. On farms, ground cover raised maize from 247 to 432 kg per hectare in Malawi's El Niño season, first-year planting-basin farmers in Zimbabwe obtained 1520 kg against 368 kg per hectare, tied ridges raised maize significantly in Tanzania, review ranges for zai and tassa pits run to 100–200% yield gains, and planting basins and direct seeding in Mozambique gave maize gains of 504 to 800 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_6, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_3]. In a Zimbabwe enterprise budget first-year planting-basin conservation farming yielded 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 400 kg on the fertilised conventional arm [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. Newer field trials add: In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, maize stalk mulch raised maize yield over no mulch at both sites in both seasons, and planting basins did so in 2012 [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_1, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_2, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_3, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_4, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_6, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_8]. In Rwanda, vetiver mulch raised maize to 8089 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_1]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by over 100 per cent on farms using zaï [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_1]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 30-cm zaï with compost gave 408 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_1]. Primary trials and surveys from eastern and southern Africa now stand in for second-hand Zambia readings. In on-farm trials in Ethiopia, ripper plus tied ridging with fertiliser gave 1775 kg of maize per hectare against 1458 under conventional maresha ploughing with the same fertiliser, and 1076 against 945 kg of tef [ev_crop_yield_rock09_1, ev_crop_yield_rock09_4]; in Tanzania, ripping and pitting combined with fertilisation gave yields 1.5–2.2 times those of conventional ploughing with the same fertilisation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and at Chipata, Zambia, basins with fertiliser gave 6660 kg of maize per hectare against 3153 under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave 3,054 kg of maize per hectare against 1,339 under ploughing, and a regression controlling for planting date, hybrid seed and fertiliser puts the gain from the basins themselves closer to 700 kg per hectare for maize and 400 to 500 kg for cotton [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_3]; a later survey of Zambian conservation-agriculture households reports 5.2 t of maize per hectare in basins against 1.8 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1]. A meta-analysis of tied-ridge-furrow experiments finds tied ridges without fertiliser or mulch yielded 17% more sorghum grain than flat planting [ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields both when rainfall was above average and during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_4, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. A review of conservation agriculture in Zambia also cites planting basins plus lime raising yields by 68% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1] and a simulated gain of around 40% for the whole conservation farming package [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, raised maize grain to 4457 kg per hectare with NPK and urea against 2157 kg under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea, and to 3768 kg averaged over the fertility options, and lifted rain water productivity from 3.10 to 6.61 kg per hectare per mm [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. Primary trials acquired in the latest round add to this: in Nigeria, averaged over four years, sorghum grain yield rose by 16% under open ridging, 25% under tied ridging and 57% under tied ridging with wood-shavings mulch, and rainfall water use efficiency rose from 1.26 kg per hectare per mm on the flat bed to 1.97 under tied ridging with mulch [ev_crop_yield_chir06_2, ev_crop_yield_chir06_1, ev_crop_yield_chir06_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_9]; Zambian basins averaged 4.4 t of maize per hectare against 1.7 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar12_1], and in Malawi conservation agriculture (planting in small holes under residue cover) gave 600 and 700 kg per hectare more grain than conventional ridge tillage, with lower yield variation [ev_crop_yield_seti18_2, ev_crop_yield_seti18_1, ev_yield_stability_seti18_3]. Nigerian sorghum under tied ridging with mulch fell below 1000 kg per hectare once in four years, against three times on the flat bed [ev_yield_stability_chir06_12]. Reviews add second-hand gains: tied ridges doubling maize yield on sandy soils in Zimbabwe (Motsi et al., 2004), tied ridging with mineral fertiliser raising maize grain yield from 1 to 6 Mg per hectare in semi-arid Tanzania (Jensen et al., 2003), tied ridges improving barley grain yield by at least 44% in northern Ethiopia (Araya and Stroosnijder, 2010), basin tillage with mulching raising maize yields by 30–50% on a South African clay (Hensley et al., 2000; Walker et al., 2005), soil bunds giving at least 30% more lowland rice in Tanzania in normal years (Raes et al., 2007), and in situ water harvesting raising yields on reclaimed degraded farmland in Burkina Faso by at least 400 kg/ha (Reij et al., 2009) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_10, ev_crop_yield_dile13_5, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_14, ev_crop_yield_dile13_7, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_9, ev_crop_yield_dile13_3, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_12, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_16, ev_crop_yield_dile13_8]. On grazing land, contour bunds in Ugandan pastures increased fodder availability (Ngigi, 2003), and saltbush planted in furrows upslope of ridges in Jordan was reported to considerably improve forage quantity and quality (Akroush et al., 2011; Al-Shamiri and Ziadat, 2012) [ev_forage_productivity_biaz12_25, ev_forage_productivity_stav20_5].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Held out of the class, as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rain exceeds 80 mm a day and 1,200 mm a year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than flat-cultivated fields because of frequent waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. In a wetter sub-humid Kenyan site, ridged plots with fertiliser gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Read these as a siting limit: in-situ capture should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. In drought seasons gains vanish: tied ridging gave no advantage in Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, and in Mozambique no cowpea yield was obtained on any treatment in a season heavily affected by drought [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_2]. Much of the pit gain depends on manure or fertiliser (pits alone gave an average sorghum gain of only 38 kg/ha in one study against 310 kg/ha in another), the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the review ranges for pits are not pooled estimates [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1]. In the Malawi El Nino survey banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare, so some in-field practices lowered yield in that season [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5]. Planting basins gave no significant gain over no mulch in 2011 at either Ethiopian site (4239 against 4171 and 4265 against 4131 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_5, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_7]. Rwandan contour ridges were not significantly different from flat rainfed plots (5937 against 4755 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_2]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. The East African and Zambian trial gains are bundles. In Ethiopia the comparator carried the same fertiliser, but without fertiliser neither improved tillage nor fertiliser alone raised maize significantly, and the 20–50% tef gain without fertiliser was not significant [ev_crop_yield_rock09_2, ev_crop_yield_rock09_3]; the Tanzanian ripping-or-pitting arms are bundled with reduced tillage [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and the Chipata basins carried improved seed against a conventional practice with extremely low fertiliser, in seasons of well-above-average rainfall, a gain the authors say cannot be fully explained [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. Some trial arms lost: pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment at Machakos, at 1.2 against 1.6 t per hectare under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9], and at the more arid Kenyan sites each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, which the treatments did not avert; water harvesting is not irrigation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The Zambian 2001/2 raw contrast is one season with no normal-year reference and mixes the basin effect with higher input use, since most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit; the regression figure is the cleaner estimate, and even its basin dummy also picks up extra weeding labour and lime [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2]. The later Zambian survey yields are farmer self-reports with large spreads, and the basin gain over ploughing (5.2 against 3.8 t per hectare) was not significant [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1, ev_crop_yield_umar11_2]; a national Zambian smallholder panel finds no significant maize yield effect of planting basins under any of its estimators [ev_crop_yield_burk12_1]; and paired soil samples on Zambian fields under basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in nitrogen [ev_soil_nitrogen_umar11_6]. The Zimbabwe panel keeps drought-season and normal-season results apart: in average rainfall periods conservation agriculture had no significant impact on any crop, in another specification it decreased maize yields by itself, and it did not mitigate rainfall-shortfall or surplus losses for millet and groundnut, so its gains appear only in seasons away from the average [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1, ev_crop_yield_mich19_2, ev_crop_yield_mich19_6, ev_crop_yield_mich19_7]. The tied-ridge meta-analysis finds no significant millet gain over flat planting and no significant difference when grass mulch was added to the ridges, and its sorghum observation count is internally inconsistent [ev_crop_yield_makm21_3, ev_crop_yield_makm21_2, ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. Farmer reports of basin yields of >1 tonnes per hectare in poor-rainfall seasons, against total failure under ploughing, compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author calls too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The remaining Zambia and global figures are cited secondhand in Arslan and colleagues' literature review, and none has a normal-year comparison: the 68% gain is for planting basins plus lime application, with timely conventional farming giving 50% in the same trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1]; and the roughly 40% gain is a simulation of the whole conservation farming package, through early planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. Readings in that review that misread their primaries were dropped, and the primaries themselves are now in the pool directly. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers the 2014 season only, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gains belong to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (3507 kg per hectare with NPK and urea, 3065 kg averaged, against 2157 kg) were not significantly different from the control in yield, nor in rain water productivity (4.84 against 3.10) [ev_crop_yield_koro17_2, ev_crop_yield_koro17_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2]. At Péni no conservation arm differed significantly from the control in yield or water productivity, grass strips with zaï giving 4192 kg and earth bunds with contour ploughing 4067 kg against 3317 kg per hectare; the authors attribute this to rainfall, saying water was not a limiting factor at Péni [ev_crop_yield_koro17_5, ev_crop_yield_koro17_6, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. The newer primaries also show where the gain fails: Nigerian open and tied ridging without mulch yielded 9 and 3% less than the flat bed in 2000, when rain failed at flowering and grain filling, and did not consistently raise water use efficiency without a residue mulch [ev_crop_yield_chir06_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_8]; in Ghana tied ridges made no significant difference to maize yield [ev_crop_yield_dalt14_1]; and in Mozambique basin and direct-seeded maize yields did not differ [ev_crop_yield_kida19_1]. Much of the size rides on mulch or fertiliser: in Nigeria mulch on a flat bed alone raised yield by 77%, more than any ridging arm [ev_crop_yield_chir06_4], and the Tanzanian tied-ridge figure compares ridges with fertiliser against flat planting without it [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_14]. The review figures are cited second-hand and several multipliers come without a baseline yield.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zai pits, planting pits, contour bunds and planting basins can raise farm income by raising yields. Returns to labour for these practices in Burkina Faso exceed the shadow wage, and bunds show returns above cost at subproject level in Mauritania [ev_economic_return_kabo04_1, ev_economic_return_mrt14_5]. In Zimbabwe, first-year planting-basin farmers earned a maize gross margin of 473.36 USD per hectare against 70.60 on conventional plots in the low-rainfall budget, with 866.84 against 357.16 for experienced farmers in high rainfall [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]. Zambian crop budgets give hand-hoe conservation-farming basins returns per hectare 70 percent higher than conventional hand hoe cultivation and 150 percent higher than conventional plowing for cotton, and returns to land and peak-season labor 60 to 90 percent higher than hand hoe tillage for maize [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_7, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]. In Zambia, partial budgets found it profitable for a household to switch to conservation agriculture, with a marginal rate of return of 860% from hand hoeing to basin digging and 360% from ploughing to basin digging [ev_economic_return_umar12_2, ev_economic_return_umar12_3]. In Mozambique basins returned $148 per hectare against $104 under conventional tillage, an imputed value of $44 per hectare for a risk-neutral farmer [ev_economic_return_kida19_2, ev_economic_return_kida19_4]. In Ghana tied ridges with grass strips gave a higher net return than flat-land maize in 2010 despite a slightly higher cost [ev_economic_return_dalt14_3], and in Nigeria wood-shavings mulch on a flat bed was expected to increase the financial benefits to farmers by 238% [ev_economic_return_chir06_11].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The evidence conflicts, and what pulls it apart is how the gain is valued and against what. Crop budgets built on bundled input packages put basins well ahead [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8, ev_economic_return_mazv09_1]; but a Zimbabwe household panel that values predicted yields with inputs held constant finds conservation agriculture generates less revenue than traditional cultivation over a large portion of the rainfall distribution [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. Other losses are season- or practice-specific: tied ridging in a Kenyan drought season, where net benefits were higher without it, and 30-cm zaï on a Burkina Faso trial, which ran at a loss of −98 624 FCFA per hectare against the experiment's own investment cost [ev_economic_return_ndun23_1, ev_economic_return_zour25h1_4]. Manual zai gives far smaller net benefits than mechanised zai [ev_economic_return_zoug14_1]. The Zimbabwe margins include manure and fertiliser and the high-rainfall figure is a sensitivity scenario [ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]; the Zambian returns are bundled with early planting and purchased inputs, which the authors say dominate the maize results [ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]; and the Zimbabwe panel figure is gross revenue with labour unvalued, so it is neither a profit nor a poverty measure [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. The newer field trials split the same way, and cost is what separates them: in Nigeria the high production costs of open and tied ridging, with or without mulch, gave net economic losses of about 1, 0.5, 11 and 12%, while mulch on the flat bed paid [ev_economic_return_chir06_10, ev_economic_return_chir06_11]; and in Mozambique basin and conventional returns did not differ significantly at intermediate elevation [ev_economic_return_kida19_3]. The Zambian rates of return come from partial budgets of a single crop, maize. Farm income and returns are proxies for poverty.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Infiltration trenches intercept and infiltrate runoff, cutting plot-level runoff and soil loss, with the runoff reduction larger on natural vegetation than on cropland [ev_erosion_hazard_locat20_1, ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_2]. Meta-analyses quantify the effect: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds soil loss cut by 68.67% under mulching and 54.97% under ridging and runoff by 57.2% and 53.6% [ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_2, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_3, ev_runoff_reduction_tefe24_2, ev_runoff_reduction_tefe24_4]; an Ethiopian synthesis reports soil loss down 59% under graded soil bunds, 88% under level soil bunds, 98% under mulch and 62% under tied ridging, with runoff down 25.2%, 60.1%, 75.5% and 55.8% [ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_1, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_2, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_4, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_5, ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_1, ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_2, ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_5, ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_4]; Lanckriet et al. (2012), cited in a Tigray review, measured soil loss of 14.4 against 35.4 t per hectare a year under moisture-conserving conservation agriculture compared with plain tillage [ev_erosion_hazard_gebr18_6]; tied ridging in India reduced runoff by 69%, tied ridges in northern Ethiopia cut runoff by about 60% (Araya and Stroosnijder 2010, cited by Biazin et al.), West African tied ridging lost 0% to 15% of seasonal rainfall as runoff against 20–40% under open ridging or flat planting (Hulugalle 1990) [ev_runoff_reduction_biaz12_7, ev_runoff_reduction_biaz12_11], contour furrow-ridge systems on Palestinian hillslopes decreased runoff by an average of 73% (Al-Seekh and Mohammad 2009, cited by Stavi et al.) [ev_runoff_reduction_stav20_4], reviews report zai and tassa pits cutting runoff by 60–80% and high mulch cover by up to 79%, and Moroccan tabia store the runoff of all rains below 50 mm [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_7, ev_runoff_reduction_ngur26_1, ev_runoff_reduction_ngur26_2, ev_runoff_reduction_roos10_1]. A meta-analysis of mulching finds runoff reduced by 47.4% and soil loss by 76.2% against controls, soil loss by 70.9% on cropland, and reductions of 45.9% and 75.1% at rainfall intensities above 90 mm/h [ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_1, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_2, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_3, ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_5, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_6].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The trench units come from a single review, largely in the Peruvian Andes (upper-middle income), which also reports increased catchment sediment in the first years after construction; plot-level effects may not transfer to catchments [ev_erosion_hazard_locat20_2, ev_erosion_hazard_locat20_3]. Tabia overflow and gully the slope in the biggest storms [ev_runoff_reduction_roos10_1]; the meta-analytic figures are unweighted means of plot studies, the pit and mulch ranges are review syntheses, and the Ethiopian, West African and Palestinian figures are citations within reviews; the Palestinian furrow-ridge systems were more effective in arid and semi-arid than in dry sub-humid areas [ev_runoff_reduction_ngur26_1, ev_runoff_reduction_biaz12_7, ev_runoff_reduction_stav20_4]. The mulching meta-analysis pools land uses including post-fire forest and bare land; cropland and tree crops were less effective in reducing runoff, both below 40%, and the mulching benefits decreased with increasing rainfall intensity under heavy rainfall [ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_4, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_6].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field bunds reduce what leaves the field in runoff: an Ethiopian synthesis finds graded soil bunds reduced the loss of soil organic matter by up to 52%, total nitrogen by up to 48% and available phosphorus by up to 41% [ev_nutrient_removal_adim16_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Confidence is very low because the row rests on a single synthesis for a single practice, graded soil bunds in the Ethiopian highlands, so the large reduction cannot be checked against any other source [ev_nutrient_removal_adim16_1]. The figures are upper bounds of nutrient loss from the field, not measured water chemistry downstream, and they say nothing about pits, basins or mulch. A project concerned with nutrient export downstream has one measured practice to go on.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Pits, basins, bunds and tied ridges catch rain where it falls and hold it in the root zone. A meta-analysis finds infiltration pits have the highest SMD of 114.4% for soil moisture retention, with tied ridging at 48.9% [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_2, ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_5]. In Burkina Faso zaï can retain moisture in the soil for seven to ten days after rainfall [ev_soil_water_retention_sawa11h1_8]; in Brazil tied furrows kept more soil moisture than the traditional flat system at all crop stages and depths [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9]; and in Ethiopia hand-dug planting basins held more topsoil water than unmulched plots at Ziway at flowering (27.4 against 25.5) and at maturity (26.5 against 25.9) [ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_4, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_6]. Mulching, the soil-cover form of in-situ water harvesting, improves soil moisture retention with an SMD of 54.0% in the meta-analysis, and maize-stalk mulch in Ethiopia held more topsoil water than unmulched plots at Ziway at each stage measured [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_4, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_3, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_5]. Water productivity, the grain produced per unit of rain, is a route by which capture eases water stress. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, lifted maize rain water productivity from 3.10 kg per hectare per mm under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea to 6.61 [ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. In a Nigerian field trial, tied ridging with wood-shavings mulch stored 8, 26 and 14.4% more soil water than the flat bed in successive seasons, and raised rainfall water use efficiency of sorghum grain from 1.26 to 1.97 kg per hectare per mm [ev_soil_moisture_chir06_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_9]. Reviews cite tied ridging, open ridging and sub-soiling improving root-zone soil water by 24%, 15% and 3% over traditional tillage in drought-stricken Wollo, Ethiopia (McHugh et al., 2007), tied ridges cutting surface runoff by about 60% and raising rooting-zone soil water by at least 13% in northern Ethiopia (Araya and Stroosnijder, 2010), and 20–25 cm deep contour furrows increasing soil moisture and shrub productivity on rangeland in Iran's Sistan Baluchistan (Jahantigh and Pessarakli, 2009) [ev_soil_moisture_biaz12_6, ev_soil_moisture_dile13_1, ev_soil_moisture_biaz12_8, ev_soil_moisture_stav20_6].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Tillage alone is not water harvesting: in the Brazilian trial deep ploughing, a tillage practice, scored as high as the tied furrows [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9]. The Brazilian trial ran a single season at a station of the agency that promotes the technology [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9]. At Melkassa the Ethiopian mulch plots differed from unmulched plots only at maturity, not at planting or flowering [ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_7, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_9, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_11]. The Ethiopian basins did not differ from unmulched plots at planting at Ziway or at any stage at Melkassa [ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_2, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_8, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_10, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_12]. Under meteorological drought and dry spells in Kenya, tied ridging without organic inputs was insufficient in soil moisture conservation since there was little or no rainwater to be held in the basins [ev_soil_water_retention_ndun23_1]. A review found no significant effect of infiltration trenches on soil moisture because only four studies provided sufficient statistical data [ev_soil_water_retention_locat20_1]. The zaï result comes with compost in the pits [ev_soil_water_retention_sawa11h1_8]. The Mauritanian well-level and Andean trench evidence now sits in the in-situ catchment water yield row, which also answers what upstream capture does to water downstream. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers a single season, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gain belongs to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (4.84 against 3.10) were not significantly different from the control, and at Péni neither grass strips with zaï (4.51) nor earth bunds with contour ploughing (4.31) differed significantly from the control (3.53), the authors stating that water was not limiting at Péni, which had more rain than Houndé that season [ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. In the Nigerian trial, open and tied ridging without mulch stored only a few per cent more soil water, significant on only one out of the nine measurement dates, and did not consistently raise water use efficiency, so ridging may not be an improvement without a residue mulch [ev_soil_moisture_chir06_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_8]. The Ethiopian and Iranian soil-moisture figures are cited second-hand.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In the humid Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where daily rains exceed 80 mm, zaï pits concentrate infiltration and sorghum in the pits yielded less than on flat-cultivated fields [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, waterlogging lasting 3–5 days during early maize growth also affected the mulching and basin treatments, whose waterlogged plants had yellow leaves and stunted growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. Primary sources from southern Africa make the same point: an FAO study shows by a water-balance calculation that planting basins can depress yields when too much water concentrates in them under high rainfall or in seasons with abnormally high rainfall, citing extension reports and farmer testimony of farmers scooping water from the basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8], and concludes that in sub-humid environments yields could be affected by water-logging in years with adequate rainfall [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. In a Kenyan on-farm trial, ridged plots with fertiliser at the relatively wetter sub-humid Rachuonyo site gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. In Tanzania, tied ridges that helped maize in years of near-normal rainfall (500–600 mm) caused waterlogging in wet years (700–900 mm) (Jensen et al. 2003, cited in a review) [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The Cameroon result is an unpublished observation cited by the authors, with no magnitude [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. The Ethiopian waterlogging finding is a field observation with no measured yield loss, and the source names a tillage treatment as the one particularly affected, so only part of the harm can be put on mulch and basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. The southern African basin finding rests on a theoretical water balance plus extension reports and farmer testimony, and the author notes there are currently few published data to substantiate it [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8]; the sub-humid conclusion goes beyond what the crop model simulates and covers conservation agriculture as basins or ripping with residue retention, so it is bundled with reduced tillage; neither gives a magnitude [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. The Kenyan ridging loss is the authors' probable explanation rather than a measured waterlogging contrast, and the ridging is bundled with fertiliser; because it comes from using the practice at a wetter site than it suits, it is held out of the production classes as an envelope misfit (a suitability caveat) and counted here as waterlogging evidence [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. The Tanzanian finding is cited second-hand and gives no yield loss [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field practices hold water where the crop grows, which backfires in wet conditions: in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rainfall exceeds 80 mm per day and 1 200 mm per year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than on flat-cultivated fields because of frequent soil waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. Primary sources from southern Africa make the same point: an FAO study shows by a water-balance calculation that planting basins can depress yields when too much water concentrates in them under high rainfall or in seasons with abnormally high rainfall, citing extension reports and farmer testimony of farmers scooping water from the basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8], and concludes that in sub-humid environments yields could be affected by water-logging in years with adequate rainfall [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. Biazin et al. cite Jensen et al. (2003) from Tanzania: tied ridges helped maize in years of near-normal (500–600 mm) rainfall, but in wet years (700–900 mm) the maize showed waterlogging effects [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: None of the harm sources gives a magnitude. The Cameroon zaï losses come from using the practice outside its rainfall window; under the standing ruling they are held out of the production classes as performance caveats, and are counted here as waterlogging hazard evidence [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. The Cameroon result is an unpublished observation cited by the authors, the Tanzanian tied-ridge result is cited from an earlier study with no yield loss stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15], and the Cameroon result rests on that one observation [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. The southern African basin finding rests on a theoretical water balance plus extension reports and farmer testimony, and the author notes there are currently few published data to substantiate it [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8]; the sub-humid conclusion goes beyond what the crop model simulates and covers conservation agriculture as basins or ripping with residue retention, so it is bundled with reduced tillage; neither gives a magnitude [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. Most units carry no farming-system tag, so the rainfed reading rests largely on the practices being field-crop techniques.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In the humid Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where daily rains exceed 80 mm, zaï pits concentrate infiltration and sorghum in the pits yielded less than on flat-cultivated fields [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, waterlogging lasting 3–5 days during early maize growth also affected the mulching and basin treatments, whose waterlogged plants had yellow leaves and stunted growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. In a Kenyan on-farm trial, ridged plots with fertiliser at the relatively wetter sub-humid Rachuonyo site gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Every unit points the same way, but none quantifies the loss, so the strength is not stated; the harm appears where in-field practices are used at wetter sites or in high-rainfall areas than they suit. The Cameroon result is an unpublished observation cited by the authors [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. The Ethiopian waterlogging finding is a field observation with no measured yield loss, and the source names a tillage treatment as the one particularly affected, so only part of the harm can be put on mulch and basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. The Kenyan ridging loss is the authors' probable explanation rather than a measured waterlogging contrast, and the ridging is bundled with fertiliser; because it comes from using the practice at a wetter site than it suits, it is held out of the production classes as an envelope misfit (a suitability caveat) and counted here as waterlogging evidence [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers for zaï or tassa pits and contour bunds in Niger rate wind velocity as reduced [ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1219_2014_wind_velocity, ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1652_2014_wind_velocity].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are practitioner ratings without stated reasoning, and the Philippine conservation-tillage compiler rates wind velocity as unchanged [ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1021_2011_wind_velocity]. No unit addresses cyclone or storm damage directly.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers for Nardi or Vallerani trenches and semi-circular bunds in Niger rate both technologies as coping well with drought [ev_asset_drought_wocat_1613_2014_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1614_2014_drought].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Both units are practitioner ratings from Niger with no observed damage data, so the row reflects compiler judgement for a single country.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers rate Nardi or Vallerani trenches and semi-circular bunds in Niger as not coping well with local rainstorms and the Vallerani system in Burkina Faso as coping moderately [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1613_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1614_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1528_2012_local_rainstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are practitioner ratings without damage records, and the compiler for mechanised Vallerani harvesting in Jordan rates coping as very good, so the outcome may depend on setting [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_5860_2021_local_rainstorm].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers rate Vallerani and Nardi trenches and semi-circular bunds in Burkina Faso and Niger as not coping well with floods [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1528_2012_flash_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1613_2014_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1614_2014_general_river_flood].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are practitioner ratings without damage records, and the compiler for mechanised Vallerani harvesting in Jordan rates coping with flash floods as very good, so the outcome may depend on setting [ev_asset_flood_wocat_5860_2021_flash_flood].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The WOCAT compiler for mechanised Vallerani micro water harvesting in Jordan rates the technology as coping very well with extreme winter conditions [ev_asset_frost_wocat_5860_2021_extreme_winter_conditions].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single practitioner rating with no observed damage [ev_asset_frost_wocat_5860_2021_extreme_winter_conditions].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In Burkina Faso the 2- and 3-m half-moon plots showed lower infiltration than the control plots, likely due to suspended matter that clogs the soil during sedimentation [ev_soil_permeability_zour25h1_8].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is one source and one trial, and the finding is for the larger (2- and 3-m) half-moons only. The authors give sedimentation as the likely cause without testing it, and the damage is reduced infiltration capacity inside the basin rather than a breach or loss of the structure [ev_soil_permeability_zour25h1_8].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers rate Nardi or Vallerani trenches and semi-circular bunds in Niger as coping well with local windstorms, and the Vallerani system in Burkina Faso as coping very well [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1613_2014_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1614_2014_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1528_2012_local_windstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: All units are practitioner ratings without observed damage.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: For the Vallerani System of tractor-ploughed micro-catchments in Burkina Faso, the WOCAT compiler reports floral diversity rising from 14 to 44 species with a high share of good forage grasses and the return of more leguminous species, an average of 14 woody species per hectare on implemented sites against 6 on control plots, and insects, birds, reptiles and mammals observed on implemented sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1528_2012_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1528_2012_animal_diversity].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This row is data deficient: both units come from a single technology sheet compiled by a practitioner, with no independent ecological survey or description of how the control plots were chosen, and no other source or country is covered [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1528_2012_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1528_2012_animal_diversity]. A second independent source or one measured finding is needed before this row can state a direction or size.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Micro-catchments raise carbon removals by growing more biomass and soil carbon on treated land: for the Vallerani System in Burkina Faso the WOCAT compiler reports biomass production 5 to 30 times that of nearby unploughed soil, on average between 1000 and 1200 kg per hectare against 70 to 110 kg on control plots [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1528_2012_biomass_above_ground_C]. A Chinese meta-analysis, available as a preprint, reports fish-scale pits raising soil organic carbon storage by 79.86% on the Loess Plateau in years 11~30 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_12].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The Burkina Faso unit is a compiler rating in which above-ground biomass stands in for carbon storage, with no measured carbon stock change [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1528_2012_biomass_above_ground_C]. The fish-scale-pit figure is from a preprint that has not been peer reviewed and is an abstract statement for the best duration window in an upper-middle-income country [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_12]. The row rests on two units from two sources, a practitioner rating and a preprint; a peer-reviewed, measured carbon stock change for micro-catchments is what is missing.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The only per-hectare cost for the micro-catchment family is the compiler's establishment cost table for mechanised Vallerani micro water harvesting in Jordan, costed on 1 ha [ev_project_cost_wocat_5860_2021_establishment].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This row is data deficient: a single practitioner-reported figure, not a market price or audited project cost, from an upper-middle-income country outside the target band [ev_project_cost_wocat_5860_2021_establishment]. A second independent cost source, ideally from a low- or lower-middle-income country, is needed before the row can say whether the cost is small or large.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The only evidence is a Kenyan field trial in which ridge-furrow rain harvesting with plastic film raised the value of total inputs by 89.9 and 94.1% over flat planting, because of extra labour and the purchase of plastic sheet [ev_project_cost_mo17_8].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: With no independent source to compare against, agreement cannot be judged; this is a thin signal rather than a settled finding. The cost rise is for ridges covered with plastic film, which is not nature-based, and the trial does not separate the cost of the film from the labour of building the ridges [ev_project_cost_mo17_8]. Cost data for micro-catchments without plastic, such as demi-lunes or Vallerani basins, would be needed to say whether the practice itself raises or lowers farm costs.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The Burkina Faso WOCAT compiler for the Vallerani System links increased vegetation cover, deep roots and water storage in the soil profile to drought resilience, reporting that in years of extreme drought plants reduced their growth but most survived, were used to feed animals and grew again in the following rainy season [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_drought_impacts].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The row rests on one WOCAT compiler rating for the Vallerani System in Burkina Faso, a practitioner judgement rather than a measurement; the compiler notes that plant growth still fell in years of extreme drought [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_drought_impacts]. No measured drought-year result for micro-catchments, and no comparison with untreated land in a drought year, is in the pool; a second independent source or one measured finding is what is missing.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Micro-catchments concentrate rain where the crop grows.
